# Step 1's flock probe releases the lock it just took, and two same-second launches collide on one log path

Found while running task #24 on 2026-10-13T03:49Z (session 20261012_204902_autonomy_1020), where the same guard+launch block was dispatched three times in one message.

Two separate weaknesses in one block, both in the Step 1 preamble that `skills/autonomy-data-pipeline` prescribes (and it is prescribed there, so the fix belongs there as well as anywhere):

1. **The probe is a test, not a serialiser.** `flock -n ~/lloyd-data/_pipeline/nightly_extraction.lock -c true` acquires the lock, runs `true`, and **releases it** on exit. Two siblings dispatched in the same second therefore each take-and-drop the lock in turn and both proceed to launch an extractor. The probe can pass twice. It is only sound against an extractor that is *already running*; it says nothing about a sibling that has not reached `acquire_single_instance_lock()` yet.

2. **The log path is not unique under same-second dispatch.** `LOG=/tmp/data-pipeline-run-$(date +%Y%m%d-%H%M%S).txt` — two launches started 90ms apart both got `20261012-204928`, so both opened the **same file** with `>`, at independent offsets. This is exactly the shape the "the log path carries this run's timestamp, and only this run writes it" rule exists to prevent (the 2026-09-14 incident, where one run reported another's `PIPELINE_RESULT`). Two processes writing one file is also how a `status=locked` line could land on top of the winner's early bytes.

# Revise retrieved memory in place from the outcome of the run that retrieved it


# Revise retrieved memory in place from the outcome of the run that retrieved it

**Source:** Discover AI — "Recurrent Harness | How AI Rewrites Its Own Memory" — https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=2Qml3VB2eDM (published 20261014); vault note [[20261014-recurrent-harness-memory-revision]]

**Area:** memory (secondary: retrieval, eval, autonomy)
**Source kind:** paper — arXiv:2610.12668, "Recurrent Harness for Agentic Continual Learning" (cs.LG, 8 Oct 2026). No code release found in the video description or transcript, so this is a mechanism to recreate, not a library to adopt.
**Approach:** experiment — measurement-only pilot first, one gated write path after.
**Effort:** M

## What it is

ReHarness's claim is that a memory bank which only ever **appends** cannot fix itself. Its loop per instance: (1) forward read — retrieve top-k reflections, act, get a reward; (2) **backward revision** — a dedicated agent post-mortems the finished trajectory and rewrites *the very reflections that were retrieved for it*, usually by adding a limiting condition ("larger first **only when** descending") rather than deleting; (3) forward write — a third agent appends only what the revision did not already cover. The guard is **source grounding**: the current trajectory is an evaluation signal *only*, and any factual edit to a past reflection must be supported by that reflection's own source trajectory, so day-10 facts cannot migrate into the day-1 record.

The Lloyd analogue of the reflection bank is the loaded memory layer (`MEMORY.md` index lines, `topics/*.md`, USER.md bullets, SKILL.md rules) plus the prefetched vault notes and facts a turn actually receives.

## Why it could improve Lloyd

The paper's failure mode is already ours, and our own learnings file is the evidence. `memory_add` appends; the correction class rules that exist were all produced by *adding a new line next to the old one* — "A landed-state sentence rots and the run that inherits it cites it instead of re-reading the tree", "A carried-forward 'still owed' claim is the least-verified sentence in th…

# Revise retrieved memory in place from the outcome of the run that retrieved it


# Revise retrieved memory in place from the outcome of the run that retrieved it

**Source:** Discover AI — "Recurrent Harness | How AI Rewrites Its Own Memory" — https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=2Qml3VB2eDM (published 20261014); vault note [[20261014-recurrent-harness-memory-revision]]

**Area:** memory (secondary: retrieval, eval, autonomy)
**Source kind:** paper — arXiv:2610.12668, "Recurrent Harness for Agentic Continual Learning" (cs.LG, 8 Oct 2026). No code release found in the video description or transcript, so this is a mechanism to recreate, not a library to adopt.
**Approach:** experiment — measurement-only pilot first, one gated write path after.
**Effort:** M

## What it is

ReHarness's claim is that a memory bank which only ever **appends** cannot fix itself. Its loop per instance: (1) forward read — retrieve top-k reflections, act, get a reward; (2) **backward revision** — a dedicated agent post-mortems the finished trajectory and rewrites *the very reflections that were retrieved for it*, usually by adding a limiting condition ("larger first **only when** descending") rather than deleting; (3) forward write — a third agent appends only what the revision did not already cover. The guard is **source grounding**: the current trajectory is an evaluation signal *only*, and any factual edit to a past reflection must be supported by that reflection's own source trajectory, so day-10 facts cannot migrate into the day-1 record.

The Lloyd analogue of the reflection bank is the loaded memory layer (`MEMORY.md` index lines, `topics/*.md`, USER.md bullets, SKILL.md rules) plus the prefetched vault notes and facts a turn actually receives.
